name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
description: Labeled subsets collected from the 80 million tiny images dataset. CIFAR-10 consists of ten classes with 6000 images in each class. CIFAR-100 consists of 100 classes with 600 images in each class.
creator: Alex Krizhevsky
rai:dataCollection: The tiny images dataset on which the experiments were based was collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU over the span of six months. They assembled it by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the lexical database WordNet, using several search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista, and kept roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. After collecting all the images for a particular search term, they removed perfect duplicates and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white. For the labeled subsets, students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset by filtering out mislabeled images associated with target classes and their WordNet hyponyms, with every submitted label personally verified by the authors.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data came from web image search results for every non-abstract English noun in WordNet, using search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista. The dataset contains 80 million colour images downscaled to 32 x 32 and spread across 79,000 search terms.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: over the span of six months
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After collecting images for each search term, perfect duplicates were removed and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels were removed. For the labeled subsets, duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm and using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs and the like. The dataset was divided into training and test sets, with the training set receiving a randomly selected 5000 images from each class.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32 x 32. The authors applied a ZCA whitening transformation to decorrelate the data and set variance in each dimension to 1. In some experiments they removed the 1000 least significant principal components by setting to zero the corresponding entries of the diagonal matrix D. They also divided 32 x 32 images into 25 non-overlapping 8 x 8 patches and created a 26th patch as an 8 x 8 subsampled version of the entire image for some experiments.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. Because each image already came with a noisy label from the search term used to find it, labelers were asked to filter out mislabeled images. Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with search terms that were WordNet hyponyms of the main search term. Labelers were instructed to reject images that did not belong to their assigned class. Criteria included that the class name should be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?', the image should be photo-realistic, should contain only one prominent instance of the object, and could be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint as long as identity was still clear. Every submitted label was personally verified by the authors.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper states that each image already came with a noisy label from the search term used to find it, and the human labeling process was used to filter out mislabeled images. Every submitted label was personally verified by the authors.
rai:dataBiases: The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, although it is described as extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. The paper also notes properties induced by how people take photographs, such as making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object.
rai:dataLimitations: The rough labels from web search are extremely unreliable. The authors note that the tiny images dataset has no reliable class labels, which makes it hard to use for object recognition experiments until labeled subsets are created. They also discuss that whitening may exaggerate the significance of some directions corresponding mainly to noise.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for unsupervised training of deep generative models on large sets of unlabeled tiny images, and the labeled subsets CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 are used for object classification experiments. The paper explicitly uses training and test splits, with 5000 training images per class in CIFAR-10.
